items.title: [pewresearch.org] Pew projects Muslims will surpass Christians globally by 2035
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Muslims are projected to become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, reaching 2.57 billion people compared with 2.52 billion Christians, according to new projections from the Pew Research Center. Both populations are expected to grow, but the Muslim population is projected to increase faster, mainly because Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children in 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women. Pew estimates there were 2.02 billion Muslims and 2.27 billion Christians in 2020. If current trends continue, the Muslim population will exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the Christian population will remain just below 3 billion. The world population is projected to grow 29% over the same period. The report models demographic patterns across 201 countries and territories, including age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching. Its projections do not account for events such as wars, epidemics or natural disasters. By 2070, sub-Saharan Africa is expected to be home to more than half of the world’s Christians, while Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population. Pew’s researchers say the projected growth is largely taking place in countries where each faith is already predominant, rather than reflecting a direct shift from one religion to the other.

items.title: [elpais.com] Journalist's murder in Costa Rica raises alarm among regional press
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri was shot dead on November 16, three days after an unknown person set fire to two cars and part of the home of Panamanian investigative journalist Rolando Rodríguez in Panama City. Following the killing in Santo Domingo de Heredia, Costa Rica, press organizations and the United Nations called for an investigation and warned of its chilling effect on journalism. Reporters Without Borders (RSF), an international organization that defends press freedom, said it had already raised the alarm about pressure on critical journalists and obstacles to reporting independently. A University of Costa Rica poll published on November 11 found that 58% of the population considers journalism dangerous to practice, and 54.7% believes freedom of expression is at risk. The Costa Rican Prosecutor's Office said it would examine Rodríguez's public allegations, the people he named, and other possible motives for the crime. It added that it seeks to identify both the perpetrators and those who ordered the killing. President Laura Fernández condemned the murder and said she had ordered the police forces to cooperate with the investigation.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

Springfield, Massachusetts, has not advanced a proposed ban; councilors plan to review possible safeguards before deciding whether to send it forward. The systems record plates, timestamps and locations. Police say they can help investigate crimes and find missing people, while privacy advocates warn about tracking, misuse and data sharing beyond local jurisdictions. Suffolk County’s sheriff’s office has data-sharing relationships with slightly more than 400 agencies, established through system settings rather than formal written agreements. Ohio lawmakers are considering House Bill 725, which would set statewide rules for police use of plate data and make misuse a fifth-degree felony. The ACLU of Ohio argues the bill regulates data only after collection and could reduce public access to search information. Springfield’s committee plans to meet again after consulting the city’s Law Department.

In Brazil, an estimated five million people remain undiagnosed, in addition to the 16 million who have been diagnosed. In Argentina, nearly four in 10 people with abnormal test results were unaware of their condition. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that more than 589 million adults worldwide are living with diabetes. Type 2 diabetes can progress for years without clear symptoms; when blood glucose remains high, it can cause cardiovascular, kidney, vision, and nerve damage. Authorities and specialists recommend screening tests, clinical follow-up, and sustained lifestyle changes. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative bloc has agreed to back Bavarian parliament speaker Ilse Aigner to succeed German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, potentially making her the first woman to hold the largely ceremonial office. Aigner, 61, belongs to the Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU’s Bavarian sister party. The CSU put her forward earlier this year, but Merz delayed backing her while considering alternatives, including Bundestag President Julia Klöckner. Support from Social Democrats and Greens, as well as CDU state leaders, grew in recent weeks. The choice followed weeks of tension between the CDU and CSU over whom to nominate. Steinmeier’s second five-year term ends in March 2027, and he cannot seek another term. Germany’s president represents the country and signs legislation, while the chancellor leads the government. Every president since the Federal Republic’s founding in 1949 has been a man.

items.title: [energytracker.asia] COP31 fossil-fuel deadlock leaves energy shift to voluntary pledges
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after the European Union and several other countries rejected a draft that omitted a direct reference to moving away from fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia and other fossil-fuel-dependent states opposed such language. Delegates adopted no new overarching political direction on fossil fuels, while separate voluntary initiatives continued, including an electrification pledge backed by more than 90 countries. A proposal to expand carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) to gigatonne scale by 2035 was also disputed. Global operating capture capacity was about 68 million tonnes a year in mid-2026, while deployment across Asia remains limited. Countries adopted a three-year extension of the Just Transition Work Programme, but the mechanism intended to put it into operation remained underdeveloped. The International Maritime Organization’s 176 member states are due to discuss a shipping emissions framework on Nov. 30 that could establish global carbon pricing and binding measures.

items.title: [pogowasright.org] Irish regulator fines Tinder owner €11 million over incomplete data access
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Match Group, the owner of dating app Tinder, €11 million on Nov. 13, ruling that Tinder’s “Download My Data” tool failed to give users adequate access to their personal data. The regulator said the tool omitted some data categories without notice and provided other information only in summary form, violating users’ access rights under the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The regulator also reprimanded Match Group and ordered it to bring its data processing into compliance within three months. DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle said tens of thousands of people used the tool during the period under review and that automated access tools must be fair and transparent about the information they provide. Match Group said it would appeal and defended the privacy protections it had built for Tinder users. The regulator’s order also requires the company to change the tool to provide relevant data and identify information it cannot supply for privacy reasons.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did. Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.

items.title: [cyberscoop.com] Kazakh ransomware suspect extradited to US in healthcare extortion case
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, was extradited from Italy and appeared in federal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on charges related to alleged ransomware attacks on U.S. hospitals, schools and healthcare providers. Prosecutors say he was part of the 8-Digits Team, a group linked to the INC and Lynx ransomware operations that breached networks, stole data and demanded payment not to publish it. The indictment says the group claimed to possess more than 50 terabytes of stolen data, including over 70 million confidential health records, and issued ransom demands totaling more than $500 million. Khlynovskiy faces charges including computer fraud, wire fraud, extortion and money laundering, as well as threats involving nonconsensual intimate images under the TAKE IT DOWN Act. If convicted on all charges, he could face up to 27 years in prison. The FBI said its investigation is continuing.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] Hackers breach U.S. spy analysis network, risking exposure of priorities
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Hackers breached an unclassified open-source intelligence analysis network used by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), exposing some information, according to people familiar with the incident. A source told The Associated Press that the breach had been resolved and involved no classified information. The network processes publicly available and commercially sourced material, including social media, satellite imagery and paid data feeds. Investigators have not identified the attacker or specified which records were exposed. Reports also indicated that the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was affected and that information at other government agencies may have been exposed. Access to analysts’ activity could reveal what U.S. intelligence agencies are tracking, even without access to classified files. Nextgov reported that investigators believe hackers used ARTEX, an AI-enabled intrusion tool, but U.S. officials have not publicly attributed the breach to a person, group or government.

items.title: [theregister.com] Web-testing platform Optimizely breach exposes visitors at 178 sites to malware
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Hackers exploited a vulnerability in website-testing platform Optimizely on Nov. 16, injecting malicious JavaScript into scripts used by 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, HSBC and Salesforce. Security researcher Scott Helme and cybersecurity firm Report URI found that the code reached visitors through Optimizely’s trusted delivery infrastructure, without requiring attackers to break into each customer’s servers. The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, capture card details entered into website forms, steal browser cookies, take screenshots and load exploit kits targeting older Apple iPhones and iPads. Report URI tracked about $7,040 in cryptocurrency sent to attacker-linked wallets in roughly nine hours. Researchers could not establish how many card details were stolen and reported no confirmed iPhone takeover in this campaign. Optimizely said it patched the flaw, removed the injected code, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts. Salesforce disabled the scripts while investigating, and IKEA opened an inquiry. Equifax stopped using the service and said it found no evidence its systems were compromised.
